idiom_name: Module + Object#extend for a per-object interface, instance variables (or ObjectSpace::WeakMap) for state
implementation_notes: Ruby's object model absorbs the pattern. Including a module in a single object's singleton class with obj.extend(TextAccessor) adds that interface to that object and to no other instance - the documentation describes extend as 'includes the given modules in the singleton class of self' - and respond_to?(:first_word) is the capability query, so no Extension base class or getExtension method is needed. State attaches just as directly as an instance variable on the same object (the module's methods read and write @words); where the object cannot hold state at all - frozen objects, immediate values such as Integer/Symbol/nil, or objects shared by Ractors - the replacement is a side table: ObjectSpace::WeakMap, whose keys are compared by identity and held weakly, or a Hash keyed by object_id with an explicit lifetime. Use refinements (Module#refine plus using) when the additional methods must reach a class without reopening it globally, and reopen the class only when the change really applies to every instance.
code_sketch:
module TextAccessor
  def words = @words ||= text.scan(/\w+/)
  def misspelled(dict) = words.reject { |w| dict.include?(w) }
end

doc = Document.new(text: "hello wrld")
doc.extend(TextAccessor)                       # this object only
doc.misspelled(dict) if doc.respond_to?(:misspelled)
pitfalls: Reopening the class is not this pattern: it changes every instance, including instances owned by code you do not control, whereas extend touches one object - but extend runs at runtime and allocates a singleton class, so calling it in a hot loop is a measurable cost.

ObjectSpace::WeakMap compares keys by identity (two equal strings are distinct entries) and holds values weakly too, so attached state disappears as soon as nothing else references it - correct for caches, wrong for data that must outlive the reference graph; it is also not enumerable for cleanup.

Frozen objects (including frozen string literals, Ractor-shared objects and many library singletons) raise FrozenError on instance_variable_set, and immediate values cannot be extended at all, so attached state has to live outside such objects.

Refinements are lexical: a method added by refine is only active inside the file or class body that activated it with using, so a capability 'added' this way is invisible to callers elsewhere - the most common reason a refinement appears not to work.
